title: Walking Floquet code circuits for zero-overhead leakage reduction
authors: Hanna Westerheim, Kaavya Sahay, Shruti Puri
abstract: Leakage, occurring when a qubit undetectably exits the computational subspace, poses a significant challenge for quantum error correction by inducing correlated errors in space and time. These correlations reduce both the code threshold and the effective code distance. To address this challenge, we introduce two zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code (hFC), termed the swirling and sliding circuits, which periodically remove leakage while dynamically protecting logical qubits via a schedule of anticommuting two-body measurements. Unlike previous dynamic circuits for the hFC, ours preserves the distance to Pauli errors. We further study their performance under leakage and find that, for two leakage noise models, they may correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors, improving on the more widely known walking surface code. Through numerical simulation, we observe that finite-error-rate performance under leakage is strongly influenced by entropic effects, producing a pronounced waterfall regime in which the logical error rate decreases much more rapidly with physical error rate than the expected distance-limited scaling. In this regime, even when asymptotic predictions suggest otherwise, the hFC can outperform the same-distance walking surface code in error rates and sub-threshold logical error scaling.
summary: This paper presents novel, zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code to combat leakage errors in quantum computation. By dynamically removing leakage while preserving code distance, the circuits show superior error correction capabilities compared to existing methods. The work highlights the importance of entropic effects, predicting a rapid 'waterfall' improvement in error rates at finite physical error levels.
main_problem: The paper addresses the significant challenge of leakage errors in quantum error correction (QEC), which induce correlated errors and degrade code performance.
main_result: The proposed zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code can correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors, and exhibit a pronounced 'waterfall regime' where performance surpasses distance-limited scaling predictions.
method: The authors introduce and analyze two specific walking circuits (swirling and sliding) designed to periodically remove leakage while dynamically protecting logical qubits using anticommuting two-body measurements.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the honeycomb Floquet code (hFC) implemented on a hexagonal lattice, analyzed under several physically motivated leakage noise models (e.g., depolarizing, skip-gate leakage).
key_observables: Logical Error Rate ($p_L$), Code Distance, Qubit Lifetime, and the scaling exponent ($\alpha$) of the error rate.
important_parameters: Physical error rate ($p$), leakage noise strength, and the comparison between asymptotic low-error regimes and finite-error 'waterfall' regimes.
main_assumptions: The circuits are designed to be 'zero-overhead,' meaning they do not require additional qubits, gates, or time steps for leakage removal.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hFC on the lattice, the four leakage noise models considered, and plots showing the dependence of the logical error rate on the physical error rate, highlighting the waterfall regime.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the hFC and the leakage problem, details the construction of the zero-overhead circuits (swirling/sliding), analyzes performance under various leakage models via numerical simulation, and compares results against the walking surface code.
why_interesting: The focus on leakage mitigation and the observation of non-standard error scaling regimes (waterfall) provide advanced insights into the practical limits of fault-tolerant quantum computation beyond simple asymptotic bounds.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The P6 honeycomb Floquet code (hFC) on the hexagonal lattice. Each panel represents the hFC at a particular point in time, where we show the evolution of a logical operator representative and the ISG. Check sets represented by the edges above the arrows are measured between time steps.

FIG. 2. The four leakage models considered in this work. The models differ in the effect of a leaked qubit on a sealed qubit upon interaction through a two-qubit Clifford CP gate, where P is a Pauli (CZ is shown as an example).

FIG. 3. Standard syndrome extraction circuit (SEC). (a) The ancilla qubit (middle wire) is reset, entangled with the two data qubits, and then measured. The measurement yields the eigenvalue of ZZ on the data qubits. (b) The standard SEC preserves data/ancilla qubit role assignments, unlike the late- and early-SWAP SECs shown in Figs. 5 and 6.

FIG. 5. Late-SWAP syndrome extraction circuit. (a) The central term is a schematic representation of the late- SWAP circuit, where just before measurement, a SWAP is applied between the ancilla qubit and one of the data qubits. The right-hand side employs Fig. 4(a) and (c), yielding the final, zero-overhead circuit. (b) The late-SWAP SEC ex- changes the roles of one of the data qubits and the ancilla, with the solid arrow indicating the direction of the data qubit information transfer.

FIG. 6. Early-SWAP syndrome extraction circuit. (a) The central term is a schematic representation of the early- SWAP circuit implementation, where a SWAP is applied be- tween the ancilla qubit and one of the data qubits just after the first CX gate. The right-hand side employs Fig. 4(b), yielding the final, zero-overhead circuit. (b) The early-SWAP SEC transfers information from one data qubit to the freshly initialized ancilla, as indicated by the dashed arrow.
